segments.text: These lenses have the same focal length. Yet their rays do not land in the same tiny spot.
One looks better at the centre of the image, but that is only one place to look.
Which lens should we build? First, we have to decide what better means.
Lens design begins with a measurable task, not a favourite shape.
Recall the ray tracer: intersect a surface, find its normal, then apply Snell's law at each boundary.
Send a bundle from one distant object point through the entrance aperture. Each ray reaches a different position on the detector.
Their mean position is the spot's centroid. Measure each ray's distance from that centre.
Square those distances, average them, and take the square root. That gives the RMS geometric spot radius.
Smaller means a tighter ray bundle, for this aperture and detector plane. It does not yet describe diffraction.
We score spread around each centroid, so image position and distortion remain separate requirements.
Now choose the design variables. Our lens has two spherical surfaces, with curvatures given by inverse radius.
Keep the glass index, centre thickness, entrance aperture, and wavelength fixed. The effective focal length stays fifty millimetres.
Change the bending parameter, q. It redistributes curvature between the two faces while we preserve the thick lens's paraxial power.
Watch the lens change shape. Its rays meet the surfaces at different angles, so their aberrations change.
Equal effective focal lengths do not guarantee equal back focal distances. The detector position is another design variable, shared by every field.
For each bending, choose one detector plane for the chosen score. Never refocus each field separately.
Begin with an object point on the optical axis. Sweep the bending and find each shape's best on-axis detector plane.
Each dot on this curve comes from an actual traced bundle. Its height is the geometric spot radius.
The lowest part identifies a promising shape. Refine the search around it instead of choosing by appearance.
This shape and detector plane reduce the on-axis spread, for the rays we have sampled.
But a good central spot is not a complete image. What happened away from the axis?
Tilt the incoming bundles to three and six degrees. First, keep the on-axis design's lens, aperture, and detector unchanged.
Now each object direction produces its own spot. Off-axis bundles can become asymmetric and need not prefer the same bending.
Use a combined merit: the mean squared spot radius over the three sampled fields, with equal weights.
Now optimize bending and one common detector plane for all three fields. Compare every resulting spot using the same scale.
The preferred lens depends on the task. Different field weights, a curved detector, or another aperture can change the answer.
An optimizer follows the score we write. It does not know which images we forgot to test.
A score also needs constraints. Reject shapes whose two surfaces collide within the required clear opening.
Require every sampled entrance ray to reach the detector. A missed surface or failed transmission must not simply disappear from the average.
Otherwise, throwing away the difficult rays could make a bad lens look excellent.
Likewise, shrinking the aperture would change the light collection and the task. We hold it fixed throughout this comparison.
Search only the feasible designs, and keep the rejected cases visible. The boundary of the search is part of the result.
Before trusting the selected lens, trace a denser pupil sample. Then test directions between the fields used in the score.
Check that the reported improvement survives. This tests sampling and generalization within our stated ray model.
It does not validate everything outside that model. Here the glass index is constant, so chromatic aberration is absent by assumption.
Nor is a cloud of ray intersections a diffraction point-spread function. Even a perfect geometric focus has a finite wave-optical spot.
Episode three supplies that diffraction scale. Episode ten explains how a chosen objective can guide many design variables with gradients.
This example searches one bending parameter and solves for a shared detector position. It is not a Maxwell adjoint optimization or a universal best lens.
Lens design is a loop: specify a task, trace the rays, measure performance, then change the prescription under constraints.
Keep the whole comparison honest: the same aperture, one shared detector plane, all tested fields, and no silently discarded rays.
The next questions are practical. What changes across colour, and what can several elements correct that one singlet cannot?
Start by asking what better means. Then build a model that can honestly answer.
